title: How well do agents use test/verification techniques?
short: Dan Luu: do testing instructions help coding agents?
author: Dan Luu (independent)
more_note: Its interactive chart (cost against fully correct runs, both efforts, hover for 50% bootstrap ellipses) and the per-condition notes are worth opening there; this page redraws the chart from its own labels and adds the significance tests the post leaves out.
takeaway: On one task (a Rust Zstd decoder written from the format spec by GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex, single-turn, 80 runs per condition and effort, judged by 37 hidden tests), a one-line instruction to use one of 26 testing or verification techniques, or one of four testing skills, did not measurably raise the share of fully correct runs over no instruction (63.8% at medium effort, 81.2% at xhigh); reading the runs, agents mostly applied each technique superficially, and the two largest skills raised cost by up to 41%.
verdict: Believe the transcript reading and the negative result: no instruction measurably helped, and the long tutorial-style skills really did cost more. Do not read the per-technique order (TDD near the bottom, the author's own skill at the top, Default "well above average") as findings: 80 runs a side detect only gaps of about 17 to 21 points, the 30 xhigh results are as alike as 30 draws of one coin, and a condition's medium score says nothing about its xhigh score. One model, one task, and no released prompts, transcripts or tests.

discussion.t: Hacker News: "How well do agents use test/verification techniques?"

responses.t: "The Hegel skill sortof sucks right now"
responses.by: David R. MacIver (Hypothesis and Hegel author), X
responses.n: Agreed the skill was weak and blamed agent-written skills in general; the post's appendix quotes him. The skill's repository was cut to "a near-empty core" on 8 September and released as version 2.0.0 on 17 September. In the author's later Pandoc runs both the old and the new skill still cost more than Hegel alone, with similar correctness.

responses.t: Without the prompts, nothing can be reproduced
responses.by: gregwebs, genxy, FranciscoCarlos and luckydata, Hacker News
responses.n: Asked for the exact prompts, the Audit instruction and the harness so others could rerun their own workflows; one called the result "essentially devoid of any value" without them. Right on the facts: no prompts, transcripts, tests or scoring code are public. jakevoytko replied with a list of what makes such benchmarks hard to publish at all.

responses.t: Left alone, the agent's Verus spec restates the implementation
responses.n: Agrees with the Verus finding and adds the case the post did not test: once a person had worked out an accurate specification, Claude proved the code against it without trouble and found real bugs. gz09 and gr_norm made the same point: a formal tool helps when a person writes the spec.

responses.t: Mutation testing as a build gate cannot be skipped
responses.by: vetronauta, kqr and coder-pm, Hacker News
responses.n: The agents did mutation testing by hand; a mutation tool wired into the build, failing it when mutants survive, is something an agent cannot quietly skip. The post tested the instruction, not the gate; coder-pm reports a gate catching a test that passed on both the fixed and the mutated code.

responses.t: Testing cannot be separated from how the code is built
responses.n: Most of effective testing is architecture (dependency injection, sans-IO), and one-shot greenfield runs with a bare instruction do not answer the title's question. yorwba answered with the post's own framing: it tests a user with no testing expertise who names a technique.

responses.t: Alloy fell on its face against fuzzing in a real project
responses.n: Longer-running use on a GPU graph-query engine agrees in direction: Alloy did badly against fuzzing even with guidance; guided fuzzing, written specifications next to the code and fresh-context adversarial review worked; one-shot auto-written skills evaluated badly.

since.n: The author's rerun with GPT-6 Astra (feed date 2 November; Hacker News 16 November, 91 points, 17 comments). Zstd is saturated (over 99% fully correct at about $1, medium). On IMAP (xhigh, 80 runs each) Default passes 76 of 80 and the four best conditions 77; all 27 are as alike as one coin (our recompute: chi-square 29.2 on 26 degrees of freedom, p = 0.30). On Pandoc (Ultra effort, 25 runs each, about $90k) many conditions sit above Default's fitted cost curve and agents finally used structured fuzzing, property-based tests and differential testing as intended; TDD again did worse, ACL2 and Proptest again did well, and the author's own skill now did worse. He calls the error bars wide and the gains plausible, not shown.
Rewritten from 8 September ("v2 draft: pare the skill to a near-empty core"), released 2.0.0 on 17 September, an adversarial-review step added in 2.1.0 on 12 October.

The Wayback Machine holds no captures of danluu.com (its index returns none and direct requests are refused) and archive.today served a captcha, so the post could not be checked for later edits; the appendix of responses was probably added after publication. The page is undated; the blog's feed gives 7 September 2026.

resources.t: What's the best programming language for coding agents?
resources.by: Dan Luu (the same eval, by language)
resources.n: Where the Zstd eval is described: the RFC plus errata, a container without internet, a decoder, hidden tests written by an agent, and the appendix listing the setup bugs fixed before the results were trusted.
The specification the agents implemented: backward-read Huffman and FSE bitstreams, the four-stream jump table, the Number_of_Sequences field.

resources.t: Agentic test processes, LLM benchmarks, and other notes on agentic coding
resources.n: The earlier post this one starts from: agents test badly by default, asking them to test more does not fix it, and skills are easy to over-read from a few runs (caveman mode).

resources.t: R1-Fuzz: Specializing Language Models for Textual Fuzzing via Reinforcement Learning
resources.n: The RL-for-fuzzing work the post cites as the exception: training a model to generate structured inputs that reach deep code paths.
The property-based testing library built on Hypothesis, and the skill the post tested at commit ef36dc6.

resources.n: Why the post's chart draws 50% bootstrap ellipses; this page uses 95% intervals and exact tests instead.
